item.content:encoded: I think the point of this is to highlight how mundane we're beginning to see things that are miracles of science. We have machines that draw organs in 3D using human tissue that can be controlled by a super computer small enough to fit in a pocket with screens that show images with dots too small for the human eye to see. We live in the future now, but no one noticed because we just use our pocket super computers to watch cats fall off of furniture. +1 to you.

item.content:encoded:
I don't know enough about bioprinting to evaluate this from an actual-science standpoint, but I dig the idea of the foundation containing things because they don't understand them, and realizing later on that they got carried away. This is a +1 for me.

It fits well into my personal canon for the foundation as a whole. They make mistakes like this for the very same reason they're able to amass world-controlling levels of power without fragmenting into smaller groups: because they're so agonizingly thorough about what they're doing that they stick to their goal regardless of context. Any person or group acting on that kind of rigidity is going to have screwups like this along the way, and seeing them have to correct it really fleshes the universe out for me.

Ultimately, this is a matter of personal opinion, but that just makes the Foundation too powerful and omnipresent for my tastes—and if they're making those sorts of decisions, too ideologically monolithic. I can't buy such a large organization not fragmenting.

Some anomalies are entire villages or tribes or even societies. Take SCP-752 for instance. They themselves are not anomalous. Deviant from the norm, but not anomalous.

Honestly, with that one I always assumed the people who created them used magic or some other anomalous method. It'd explain how they managed to do so at least a century ago, and why the scientists responsible lived for at least 70 years after the start of their experiment.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I have to agree with Roget and Scorpion.

The Foundation is, for all intents and purposes, the Illuminati. They're not against progress, because progress is considered normal, but a catastrophically disruptive tech boom is something to be actively avoided.

Yes, there is a degree of capriciousness to these judgements, and ultimately it's a bald guy at a desk deciding what's okay and what's not, but that's how they roll.

Should they have prevented the development of nuclear weapons? How do you know they didn't contribute to their development to ensure an Allied victory? Sounds like the kind of thing they would do. Preserving Colonialism may have been seen as not worth the effort. Remember, the Foundation is coldly practical. If preserving something will cost them more than it's worth, they're not going to do it. As for Russia/Soviet Union, they likely wouldn't have cared about a peasant uprising in a then backwater country, and the end of the Cold War would have been viewed as a good thing. Again, these are judgement calls being made by a bald guy at a desk, and you may not agree with him, but he's still going to do it.

As for your second point, the Foundation does contain People of Interest, not all of whom are anomalous (Dick C Normus, for instance) and no small number of whom are out for power, political or otherwise. Some anomalies are entire villages or tribes or even societies. Take SCP-752 for instance. They themselves are not anomalous. Deviant from the norm, but not anomalous. Neither they nor their tech are supernatural, but the Foundation keeps their city under lock and key because of how disruptive their existence would be.

Finally, 'Bonkers' may be vague, but in this sense super advanced tech is like porn: hard to define, but you know it when you see it. I stand by my previously made points.

item.content:encoded:
The article also states that the technology was considered anomalous, though. We're given no indication of why that is, and "It would be bonkers" doesn't cut it.

The thing is, 20 years ago this was at best vaguely plausible comic-book science: tech you'd see alongside fusion reactors and sapient AI. I could give you a dozen reasons why this technology shouldn't work… most of which have been addressed in the past couple years by breakthroughs that sound like stuff straight out of Prometheus Labs. For instance, a proprietary protein slurry harvested from a line of mouse cancer cells that just happens to be an ideal media for tissue culturing.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
If the Foundation was in the habit of doing these sorts of things, they'd be regularly intervening in non-anomalous affairs in order to keep things "normal." You'd have them working to prevent cultures from changing because they saw the new state as abnormal; they'd regularly intervene in governments to try and keep "abnormal" politicians from gaining power. Should the Foundation have prevented both World Wars because of the political and economic disruption they caused? What about the decline of colonialism, or the Russian Revolution, or the fall of the Soviet Union? Did the Foundation try and fail to contain the knowledge of nuclear weaponry?

This exact thing is definitely a large part of how I see the Foundation. These forces have either been unleashed or failed to be through direct action or inaction.

item.content:encoded:
Keep in mind that the Foundation's explicit goal is to preserve normalcy. That means keeping super-advanced tech secret even if it's not necessarily anomalous because it would be extremely disruptive to the status quo.

If the Foundation was in the habit of doing these sorts of things, they'd be regularly intervening in non-anomalous affairs in order to keep things "normal." You'd have them working to prevent cultures from changing because they saw the new state as abnormal; they'd regularly intervene in governments to try and keep "abnormal" politicians from gaining power. Should the Foundation have prevented both World Wars because of the political and economic disruption they caused? What about the decline of colonialism, or the Russian Revolution, or the fall of the Soviet Union? Did the Foundation try and fail to contain the knowledge of nuclear weaponry?

They'd also have to define when society was "ready" for this new technology, and we're given absolutely no insights into why the Foundation considers it acceptable to allow the tech to exist in 2007 after classifying it as an SCP object in… well, we don't actually know when the device was found.

If someone invented a Star Trek-like nanofactory tomorrow, even if they could explain how it worked perfectly and the Foundation confirmed it all via their own research, they would still lock it and its inventor up because of the insane political and economic disruption suddenly introducing that level of tech would cause.

The article also states that the technology was considered anomalous, though. We're given no indication of why that is, and "It would be bonkers" doesn't cut it.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I get that Prometheus Labs was significantly ahead of conventional technology. What I don't get is why it was ever classified as *anomalous*—was the Foundation incapable of building more and later found out it was because the notes were incomplete or damaged in some fashion? Does biological 3D printing go against an established scientific theory that has since been overturned?

If the Foundation's scientists can figure out how it works and explain how it works in a way that doesn't violate any well-established scientific theory, it shouldn't be considered anomalous. And if they can't, the Foundation should intervene and classify Organovo's machine as an SCP.

Alternatively, the Foundation might declare the machine to be a result of an SCP (perhaps Prometheus got their knowledge from sources that were actually anomalous), but we aren't given any information into what led them to arrive at that conclusion.

item.content:encoded: Excellent. It's a little simplistic but I think that works to its benefit - whereas you could've got this bogged down in sidestories and intrigue it's a pretty effective proof-of-concept for the human race catching up to the Foundation's rate for reality-fuckery. That's what appeals to me the most about this: the way it catalogs the tech's treatment from inception to standardization feels really tight. The article's short, and some of the end bits feel a little disconnected from the overall experience - in particular, tying the achievement to one specific fictional mega/corp felt a little disingenuous, though that was offset by the way you included various other institutions, and as a whole I really liked it.

item.content:encoded:
To use a GOC lens here,

At the time that these bioprinters were recovered, shortly following the effective destruction of Prometheus Labs (in the 90s or early turn of the millennium), such advances, particularly within the field of stem cell manipulation and artificial cellular superstructure construction, would be seen as too advanced for the rest of the world to know, and would have been classified as +2Gen: too advanced for the rest of the world to know and utilize at this time. This would've held until recently (within the last 5-10 years), particularly with the expiration of the FDM patent.

In 1989, S. Scott Crump patented the (then-unnamed) Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) process that is common to most 3D printers today1. This provided the Foundation with an effective buffer - with a monopoly on one of the key components critical to the bioprinter concept, any attempt at uncontained replication of the technology was effectively shut down. This gave the Foundation years to test what they possessed, which also matched development of mechatronics and cellular biology/biomedical engineering.

In 2007, Organovo was created2, which specialized in a method of creating 3D biological prints for experimentation, which effectively downgraded the +2Gen rating to +1Gen - advanced, but not so farfetched to seem anomalous anymore. It took years for conventional human understanding to catch up, but in 2007, the knowledge base finally caught up with what the Prometheus Labs researchers were conceiving decades before.

With the expiration of the FDM patent in 20093, other companies began to get involved, effectively turning additive manufacturing as a whole to current generation status (Gen0) and progressing 3D bioprinting itself from cutting edge to more conventional status - still at +1Gen, but becoming more understandable and progressing to Gen0 status. The research put into stem cells and cellular manipulation would also serve to make such devices conventional now.

Footnotes
1. https://lawitm.com/3d-printing-law-trademarks-why-fdm-isnt-for-everybody/
2. http://organovo.com/about/about-organovo/
3. https://techcrunch.com/2016/05/15/how-expiring-patents-are-ushering-in-the-next-generation-of-3d-printing/
